newsitem.title: USA: No underlying price pressure in US CPI - Labor Dept.
newsitem.headline: No underlying price pressure in US CPI - Labor Dept.

text.p: There appeared to be no underlying price pressures in February's consumer price index and food and energy prices should be better behaved this year than last, Labor Department economist Patrick Jackman said.

"I would concur with the overall opinion here, that there doesn't appear to be any underlying price pressures that would lead one to believe that there's going to be any sort of acceleration in prices, at least in the very short run," Jackman told Reuters Financial Television.
The Labor Department had earlier reported the February Consumer Price Index rose 0.3 percent versus the 0.1 percent January increase.
The so-called core CPI, excluding volatile food and energy price, rose 0.2 percent in February, compared to 0.1 percent in January.

Jackman saw good news on both the food and energy fronts, with crude oil prices declining from their runup last year and vegetable supplies returning to normal after the January freeze in Florida. "Certainly by April you'd expect to see an easing of that (vegetable) price," Jackman said.
Crude oil prices had fallen about three dollars a barrel and only a small part had so far been passed on to consumers, Jackman said.
He cautioned that if gasoline prices did not drop soon then the start of the summer driving season would see gasoline prices eventually rise again.

But over the next few months, seasonal adjustment of the data would actually help gasoline prices. "So, say, next month if gasoline prices were unchanged we'd actually see the index on a seasonally adjusted basis fall five tenths (of a percentage point)," Jackman said.
"One looks for much better behaviour in the areas of food and energy this year than the upward blips that we had last year," Jackman said.
The reinstatement of the 10 percent airline ticket tax on March 7 would likely affect travel costs in next month's data.
"There should be some noticable impact on airline fares. Probably a turnaround from the sharp declines we experienced in January and February..," Jackman said.
